In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel therapeutic approaches for neurodegenerative diseases of the retina, such as retinitis pigmentosa, glaucoma, and age-related macular degeneration.
the development and use of human embryonic stem cells (hESC) as a potential source of cells for cell replacement therapy of retinal degenerations.
the use of hESC-RPE cells as a potential therapy for age-related macular degeneration and Stargardt disease, and hESC-RPE/choriocapillaris constructs for retinal degenerative diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the subretinal space is the most appropriate location for hESC-RPC transplantation for the treatment of retinal diseases.

the epiretina niche is more favorable for retinal cell integration and survival than the subretinal niche, but that the subretinal space is more favorable for photoreceptor differentiation than the epiretial niche.

hESC-RPC transplantation into the subretina of immunodeficient mice can result in the survival and differentiation of cells with a mature photoreceptor phenotype, and that these cells can structurally integrate into a host retina with limited synaptogenesis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

(i) hESCs can be directed in vitro to RPCs and that (ii) these cells can be transplanted into the retina of young adult mice without immunosuppressive treatment, and (iii), the grafts can mature in the host retina and integrate into the host retinal layers.
the epiretina niche can promote retinal cell integration and survival without immunosuppressive drugs, but not maturation, while the subretinal niche promotes maturation but not integration.
the hESC-RP cells can be efficiently generated from the NIH-maintained hESCs TE03 and UC-06.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the subretinal space is not an ideal niche to integrate hESC-RPC-derived NR into the host retina, and epiretinality is the best option for this purpose.
subretinal grafting of hESC-RP cells can promote their maturation to recoverin-positive phenotype in a xenogeneic environment, and this can be accomplished without the need for immunosuppression.
the subretinal niche is more conducive to photoreceptor differentiation and integration than the epiretiral one.
